name: Determining the Weather Condition (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that determines whether it is both too hot and too dry based on the inputs that it receives from the user.
code:
#Step 1: Read the user input for determining whether it is too hot
text = input("Enter 1 if it is too hot, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 2: Determine whether it is too hot
if input_num == 1 :
    too_hot = True
else:
    too_hot = False
#Step 3: Read the user input for determining whether it is too dry
text = input("Enter 1 if it is too dry, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 4: Determine whether it is too dry
if input_num == 1 :
    too_dry = True
else:
    too_dry = False
#Step 5: Write the boolean expression to determine whether it is both too hot and too dry
result = too_hot and too_dry
#Step 6: Print the result
if result == True :
    print("Yes! It is too hot and too dry.")
else:
    print("No! the weather condition 'too hot and too dry' is not met.")

2.content: text = input("Enter 1 if it is too hot, otherwise enter 0:")
commentList: Purpose: This line shows the prompt "Enter 1 if it is too hot, otherwise enter 0:" to the user and saves whatever the user types (as text) into the variable named text so you can use it later.
Syntax: text is the variable name, = is the assignment operator, and input(...) is a built-in function that takes the prompt string in quotes and returns the user's response as a string.
Behavior: input(...) stops the program and waits for the user to type something and press Enter. The returned string contains exactly what the user typed (except the Enter key), including any spaces.
Relation to later code: This line only collects a string. You convert that string to an integer on the next line (int(text)); until you convert it, comparisons with numbers will not work as intended.

Common errors and misconceptions: If the user types letters, symbols, or nothing, the later conversion int(text) will raise a ValueError. If the program runs where no interactive input is available, input(...) can raise an EOFError. Also, if the user types a digit other than 0 or 1, the program will accept it but the logic (input_num == 1) may not behave as you expect.

Best practices: Make the prompt clear and include an example or allowed values. Validate and sanitize the response before converting (for example, use text = text.strip() and check text in ('0','1')). Wrap int(...) in try/except or loop until the user gives valid input. Consider using a more descriptive variable name like hot_input to avoid confusion if you reuse text for other prompts.
